task: Apply a four-lens moral test, handle gift and payment cases, audit a supplier sample and design a code with conduct-linked pay.
condition: Given dilemma cases, a gift limit, an audit sample and a bonus plan. All money figures are in one currency of your choice.
standard: Each case is decided with stated reasons, audit figures are correct and the code separates fixed from local rules.
who: Managers who work in countries with different norms and must keep one standard.

modules.title: Four lenses for a moral choice
modules.intro: A hard choice can be viewed through results, duties, fairness and care. Using all four stops a person from relying on a single habit.
points: Results: who gains and who is harmed
Duty: which rule or promise applies
Fairness and care: who is left out
modules.example: Worked-example figures, in your currency. A plant manager must decide whether to keep a line running with a known fault. Results: running earns 40,000 a week, but 3 workers face a risk of injury. Duty: the safety rules say stop. Fairness: the workers did not choose the risk. Care: the 3 workers have families. Three of four lenses say stop, so the line is stopped, and the loss of 40,000 a week is treated as a cost of doing the job properly.
modules.activity: Take a real or case dilemma and write one sentence under each of the four lenses, then state the decision.
modules.standard: All four lenses are used and the final choice follows the majority of lenses with a reason for any lens that is overruled.

modules.title: Moral norms that differ between countries
modules.intro: Some practices are normal in one place and a crime in another. A manager must know which differences are real customs and which are just excuses.
points: Separate custom from corruption
Ask what the local law says
Ask what the home law says
modules.example: Worked-example figures, in your currency. In a host country, a small present of about 20 is given at a festival. The home-country rule sets a gift limit of 50 and needs a log entry. The present is 30 under the limit, so it is only logged. Later a supplier offers a 'thank you' of 2,000 during a contract talk. That is 40 times the limit and is linked to a decision, so it is refused and reported.
modules.activity: List three gifts with value and timing. For each, say allowed, allowed with a log, or refused, using a 50 limit.
modules.standard: Each gift is placed in the correct class using the limit and the timing of the decision.

modules.title: Gifts, facilitation payments and bribery
modules.intro: A bribe is a payment to get an unfair gain. A small payment to speed up a normal service is still risky and is banned in many places.
points: Test: is it a gain the payer has no right to?
Never pay to skip a rule
Record and report every request
modules.example: Worked-example figures, in your currency. A shipment is held at a border and an officer hints that 150 will release it today. Waiting costs 400 a day in storage for 3 days, which is 1,200. The payment is cheaper at 150, but it is still a bribe. The manager refuses, asks for the official fee list and files a request, and logs the incident. The cost to the firm is 1,200 and the firm keeps its licence.
modules.activity: Work through a case where a payment saves money. List the cost of refusal and the risk of paying.
modules.standard: The cost of refusal is calculated, the payment is named as a bribe and a lawful route is chosen.

modules.title: Labour standards in supply chains
modules.intro: A firm is responsible for how its suppliers treat workers. A simple audit checks pay, hours, age and safety.
points: Set a minimum standard in every contract
Audit a sample of sites
Fix first, end the contract last
modules.example: A firm has 40 suppliers and audits 25% each year, which is 10 sites. At the 10 audited sites, 3 show hours above the firm's limit of 60 a week. That is 30%. If the same rate applies to all 40, about 12 suppliers may break the rule. The firm gives each of the 3 a 90-day fix plan and re-audits. Any site that fails again is dropped.
modules.activity: Take 30 suppliers and a 20% audit sample. Work out the sample size, the failure rate and the likely total number failing.
modules.standard: Sample size is 6, the failure rate is calculated from the findings and the projection to 30 is shown.

modules.title: A repeatable test for a hard decision
modules.intro: A written test helps people decide the same way each time. It can be used in any country.
points: Check law, then policy, then conscience
Ask if you would be happy to see it in the news
Ask a colleague before acting
modules.example: Worked-example figures, in your currency. A sales lead may offer a customer a 12% discount, but the limit is 10%. Law: no breach. Policy: breached by 2 points. News test: a 12% discount for one buyer and 10% for others looks unfair. The lead asks the director. The deal is 500,000, so 2 points is 10,000. The director refuses the extra 2%, and the lead offers 10% plus free delivery worth 3,000.
modules.activity: Write a three-step test and apply it to a case with a number limit that is breached.
modules.standard: The test has three steps in order, the money effect is calculated and the choice stays inside the policy.

modules.title: Codes of conduct that work in many places
modules.intro: A code sets one global floor and lets local teams add detail. It must be short enough to read and clear enough to apply.
points: Global floor that cannot be changed
Local detail that cannot lower the floor or lift a ceiling
Plain words in each language
modules.example: Worked-example figures, in your currency. A firm writes a code with 8 rules. 5 are fixed globally (bribes, safety, child labour, fair pay, records). 3 can be set locally (gift limit up to the global ceiling of 50, working hours within the local legal limit, holiday gifts). A site sets a gift limit of 30, which is below the global ceiling of 50, so it is accepted. Another site sets 80, which is above the ceiling, so it is rejected.
modules.activity: Write a code with five fixed rules and three local rules and test it with two local proposals.
modules.standard: The code separates fixed and local rules and the two proposals are checked against the ceiling.

modules.title: Training and incentives
modules.intro: People follow what is rewarded. If bonuses reward only sales, staff may bend the rules, so bonuses must include conduct.
points: Pay for how as well as how much
Train with real cases
Test understanding after training
modules.example: Worked-example figures, in your currency. A sales bonus is 10,000 for hitting target. The firm changes it to 8,000 for results and 2,000 for passing a conduct review, which is 20% of the bonus. Of 50 staff, 46 pass a short case test, which is 92%. The 4 who fail redo the training in 30 days. The firm checks that conduct complaints fall from 9 to 5 in a year.
modules.activity: Redesign a 12,000 bonus so that 25% depends on conduct and set a pass mark for the case test.
modules.standard: The split is 9,000 and 3,000, a pass mark is stated and one result is tracked.

modules.title: Monitoring and reporting concerns
modules.intro: A rule with no checks is only words. Monitoring means sampling, reporting lines and a record of action.
points: Check a sample of cases each quarter
Offer a private reporting line
Log what was done and by when
modules.example: Each quarter the ethics team checks 5% of 1,200 expense claims, which is 60 claims. 3 claims break the gift rule, a rate of 5%. That projects to 60 claims out of 1,200, if all were checked. The team follows up the 3 within 14 days and logs each outcome. The following quarter the rate drops to 2 of 60, or 3.3%.
modules.activity: Take 800 claims and a 7.5% sample. Work out the sample, the failure rate for 4 breaches and the projection.
modules.standard: Sample is 60, failure rate is 6.7% and the projection is about 53 claims.

quiz.q: List the four lenses used to view a moral choice.
A gift limit is 50. A supplier gives a gift worth 35 at a festival. What do you do?
quiz.a: It is under the limit, so it is allowed, and it is logged if the policy needs a log.

quiz.q: A border officer asks for 200 to release goods. Storage is 300 a day for 2 days. Is paying right?
quiz.a: No. It is a bribe even though paying (200) costs less than waiting (600).

quiz.q: A firm audits 20% of 50 suppliers and finds 4 failures in the sample. What is the failure rate?
In the three-step test, which step comes first?
A local team proposes a gift limit of 90 when the global ceiling is 50. What happens?
quiz.a: It is rejected, because local rules cannot lift the global ceiling.

quiz.q: A 10,000 bonus has 20% tied to conduct. How much is that?

quiz.a: Because people repeat what is rewarded, so pay for results alone can push staff to break rules.

quiz.q: A 5% sample of 2,000 claims finds 6 breaches. What is the sample and the failure rate?
quiz.a: Sample is 100 and the rate is 6%.

quiz.q: A site works a 65-hour week and the standard is 60. What does the firm do first?
quiz.a: Give a fix plan with a time limit and re-audit, and end the contract only if it fails again.

ladder.title: L1 Basic: Why ethics at work
ladder.slide: A slide shows one case where a cheap choice led to a high later cost.
ladder.notes: Say: ethics is part of the job, not an extra. Check: ask for one example from the group. Mistake: treating it as a matter of opinion only.

ladder.title: L2 Basic: The four lenses
ladder.slide: Four boxes for results, duty, fairness and care sit around one dilemma.
ladder.notes: Say: use all four. Check: fill the boxes for a case. Mistake: using only the result lens.

ladder.title: L3 Core: Custom or bribe
ladder.slide: A table lists gifts by value and timing with allowed, log or refuse.
ladder.notes: Say: size and timing matter. Check: sort three gifts. Mistake: calling a bribe a custom.

ladder.title: L4 Core: Pressure payments
ladder.slide: A cost sum compares the bribe, the delay and the legal route.
ladder.notes: Say: cheaper is not the test. Check: work out the cost of waiting. Mistake: paying to save a small delay.

ladder.title: L5 Applied: Supplier audits
ladder.slide: A sample sum shows sites audited, failures found and a projection.
ladder.notes: Say: sample, then project, then fix. Check: ask for the projected number. Mistake: ending contracts before offering a fix.

ladder.title: L6 Applied: Codes and incentives
ladder.slide: A code with fixed and local rules sits beside a bonus split.
ladder.notes: Say: pay what you want to see. Check: split a bonus. Mistake: a code that nobody can read.

ladder.title: L7 Advanced: Monitoring
ladder.slide: A trend of sample failure rates over four quarters is shown with follow-up times.
ladder.notes: Say: check, record, follow up. Check: ask what trend means success. Mistake: running a check once and stopping.

rubric.meets: Uses four lenses and states a decision.
rubric.exceeds: Also explains why one lens was overruled.

rubric.not_yet: Mixes up custom, gift and bribe.
rubric.meets: Sorts cases correctly using a limit and timing.
rubric.exceeds: Also prices the cost of refusing.

rubric.meets: Sample, rate and projection are correct.
rubric.exceeds: Also sets a follow-up plan with dates.

rubric.not_yet: Code is vague or bonus ignores conduct.
rubric.meets: Code has fixed and local rules and a conduct share in pay.
rubric.exceeds: Also tracks a result after one year.

jobs.what: Writes the code and runs checks.
Applies the code and handles pressure from local partners.
Builds case training and tests understanding.
